 Florida’s $15 minimum wage 
 What does it mean for the Treasure Coast 
 By Brian Bauer
newstc@hometownnewsmediagroup.com 
 Oct 25, 2026 
 20 hrs ago

 Florida reached a significant milestone on Sept. 30 when the state’s minimum wage increased to $15 per hour. The increase marks the completion of a series of annual adjustments approved by Florida voters in 2020.
 CareerSource/For Hometown News 
 Brian Bauer

 Save 
 Florida reached a significant milestone on Sept. 30 when the state’s minimum wage increased to $15 per hour. The increase marks the completion of a series of annual adjustments approved by Florida voters in 2020.
 For an employee working 40 hours a week, year-round, the latest $1 increase represents an additional $2,080 annually before taxes, assuming their hours remain unchanged. That’s meaningful money for a household managing groceries, housing, transportation and other everyday expenses.
 The impact reaches well beyond individual paychecks. Throughout Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties, employers, consumers and job seekers are all affected by changes in the cost of labor.
 At CareerSource Research Coast, we work with businesses and job seekers every day. From that perspective, there are four important questions worth examining.
 What does the increase mean for workers and employers?
 Higher wages can help families manage household expenses and may reduce the need to work additional hours or multiple jobs.
 For employers, particularly small businesses in hospitality, retail, restaurants and service industries, the calculation is more complicated.
 Consider a business with 10 employees earning the previous $14 minimum wage, each working 40 hours a week. Raising those wages by $1 adds $400 to its weekly payroll, or $20,800 annually, before additional payroll-related expenses.
 Businesses may also face pressure to adjust wages for experienced employees already earning slightly above minimum wage.
 However, higher wages can bring benefits to employers, too. Competitive compensation can help attract qualified applicants, improve employee retention, and reduce the costs associated with recruiting and training replacements.
 Will businesses raise prices or change hiring practices?
 Some price adjustments are possible, particularly in industries where labor represents a significant share of operating expenses.
 A local restaurant, for example, must balance food costs, rent, utilities, insurance and employee wages when setting menu prices. An increase in any of those expenses can affect what customers ultimately pay.
 But raising prices is not the only option. Businesses may look for opportunities to improve productivity, adjust schedules or reduce other expenses.
 Higher wages can also put more spending money into the hands of local workers, potentially benefiting the same businesses facing increased payroll costs.
 The actual impact will vary considerably from business to business. A company already paying above $15 per hour may experience little direct change, while another operating on narrow margins may face difficult decisions.
 Will job seekers benefit, or could opportunities become harder to find?
 For individuals entering the workforce, a $15 starting wage can make employment more financially rewarding.
 At the same time, employers managing higher labor expenses may become more selective when filling positions. Some may place greater emphasis on experience, reliability, customer service, technical abilities and other workplace skills.
 That makes workforce preparation increasingly important.
 Whether someone is searching for a first job, returning to employment or considering a career change, developing marketable skills can improve their opportunities.
 At CareerSource Research Coast, we help job seekers strengthen resumes, prepare for interviews, explore training opportunities and connect with employers. We also work directly with businesses to understand their workforce needs and help them recruit and develop qualified employees.
 What can we expect in the years ahead?
 Economists have studied minimum-wage increases for decades, and their findings are not always the same. A 2024 review by economists Arindrajit Dube and Ben Zipperer, published through the National Bureau of Economic Research, examined findings from 88 studies and concluded that employment effects have generally been relatively modest.
 Other researchers have reached more cautious conclusions. In a 2022 study published in the journal Industrial Relations, economists David Neumark and Peter Shirley found that employment effects were more often negative, particularly for teenagers, young adults and less-educated workers.
 Together, these studies illustrate why the long-term effects of Florida’s minimum-wage increase cannot be predicted with certainty. Higher earnings may benefit workers and strengthen local spending, while employers may respond by adjusting hiring, staffing, prices or operating practices. The extent of those changes will depend on individual businesses and broader economic conditions.
 Florida’s scheduled annual $1 increases have now concluded. Beginning in 2027, the state will calculate future minimum wage adjustments based on inflation, with the first adjusted rate taking effect January 1, 2028.
 Ultimately, the success of our regional economy depends on businesses remaining competitive and residents having access to meaningful employment.
 As our labor market continues to evolve, education, training and partnerships between employers and workforce organizations will remain essential.
 At CareerSource Research Coast, we are committed to helping both sides of that equation succeed.
 For information about employment, training, and business services, visit www.careersourcerc.com .
 Brian Bauer is the president and CEO of CareerSource Research Coast.
